Family Assistance Legislation Amendment (Child Care Measures) Bill 2014 - Second Reading - Read a second time

This division relates to the Policy _[For limiting availability of welfare payments](/policies/34)_. The majority voted against an amendment to the original motion, introduced by Greens Senator Sarah Hanson-Young. The original motion was "that the bill be now read a second time"(Read more about the stages that a bill must pass through to become law [here](http://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). ) to which Senator Hanson-Young moved the following amendment: _At the end of the motion, add:_ _but the Senate is of the opinion that, rather than punishing families, revenue should be raised from big miners, bankers and polluters through:_ _(a) applying a 'public insurance' levy on the big four banks that are too big to fail;_ _(b) removing fossil fuel subsidised fuel for big mining companies;_ _(c) retaining the billions in revenue from the carbon price;_ _(d) implementing the original super profits mining tax;_ _(e) imposing a millionaires tax;_ _(f) taxing discretionary trusts as corporations; and_ _(g) imposing a levy on thermal coal imports exports._ Because the majority voted against this amendment, it was unsuccessful _Background to the bill_ The [bill](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/Bills_Search_Results/Result?bId=r5271) was introduced primarily to amend the [A New Tax System (Family Assistance) Act 1999](http://www.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/antsaa1999357/) in order to: - maintain the indexation pause on the [Child Care Rebate](http://www.humanservices.gov.au/customer/services/centrelink/child-care-rebate) (CCR) limit at $7500 for three years from 1 July 2014; and - maintain the [Child Care Benefit](http://www.humanservices.gov.au/customer/services/centrelink/child-care-benefit) (CCB) income thresholds at the amounts applicable as at 30 June 2014 for three years from 1 July 2014. Normally, the CCR limit and CCB income test thresholds are indexed on an annual basis to the Consumer Price Index (CPI).

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](http://www.openaustralia.org/senate/?id=2014-06-23.24.1) to read the bill for a third time.(Read more about the stages that a bill must pass through to become law [here](http://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). ) This means that the majority agree with the bill and want it to pass through the Senate. The bill will now be returned to the House of Representatives for them to consider the [amendment](http://www.openaustralia.org/senate/?gid=2014-06-23.21.2) agreed to in the Senate during the in committee stage.(See the transcript for the in committee stage [here](http://www.openaustralia.org/senate/?id=2014-06-23.21.1). ) The amendment removed all references to the [Child Care Benefit](http://www.humanservices.gov.au/customer/services/centrelink/child-care-benefit) in the bill. Introduced the Family Assistance Legislation Amendment (Child Care Measures) Bill 2014, freezing childcare benefit thresholds and the $7,500 rebate cap to save $230 million, and said an independent review found Labor's Early Years Quality Fund would have benefited less than 30 per cent of long day care workers before redirecting over $200 million to broader professional development.

Moved an amendment opposing the Child Care Measures Bill, arguing the government's paid parental leave scheme offers $50,000 cheques to millionaires while cutting childcare benefit for families earning as little as $42,000, and citing $230 million in cuts that the department says will affect around 500,000 families.

Argued the bill will strip $230 million from childcare benefit assistance relied on by over 889,000 families, said research shows every one per cent rise in childcare fees cuts mothers' workforce participation by 0.7 per cent, and noted 180 early childhood educators are leaving the underpaid sector every week.

Argued in support of the Child Care Measures Bill, detailing net savings of $105.8 million from freezing the childcare rebate and $230.4 million from freezing the childcare benefit, and said Labor had promised 260 new childcare centres but delivered only 38.

Defended the Family Assistance Legislation Amendment (Child Care Measures) Bill 2014, which freezes the $7,500 childcare rebate limit and childcare benefit income thresholds for three years to save $230 million, saying childcare fees had risen 50 per cent nationally during Labor's six years in government.

Opposed the Family Assistance Legislation Amendment (Child Care Measures) Bill 2014, saying it would strip $230 million from means-tested childcare benefits affecting 889,000 families, and that 74,000 families would reach the childcare rebate cut-off in 2014 alone.

Opposed the Family Assistance Legislation Amendment (Child Care Measures) Bill 2014, saying it would cut $336 million from childcare support and leave over 500,000 families worse off, and cited a Grattan Institute study estimating Australia's economy could be $35 billion better off if it matched Canada's childcare-driven workforce participation.

Opposed the Family Assistance child care bill, citing Goodstart research that children who miss preschool are 50 per cent more likely to be developmentally vulnerable, and calculated the bill's $76.9 million saving is only about 1.5 per cent of what the government's Paid Parental Leave scheme would cost in a year.

Opposed the Family Assistance child care bill, citing Early Childhood Australia modelling that a family earning $60,000 with one child in care would be $1,800 a year worse off by 2016-17, and described the threat to Nikinpa Aboriginal Child and Family Centre in his Charlton electorate from a $78 million annual cut to Indigenous child and family centres.

Said the government is increasing overall childcare assistance to $28½ billion over four years for about a million families, defended maintaining childcare benefit thresholds and pausing the childcare rebate limit at $7,500 per child for three more years as a Labor-originated measure, and said childcare fees rose 53 per cent under the previous government.
